intro.heading: The error is handled. The question is what it tells you.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: On a Tuesday morning, a senior notices a gap on a MAR chart and finds a dose was given late the night before. The manager speaks to the carer, follows the home's medicines error procedure and makes sure the person is safe. The matter feels closed. Then a quieter worry arrives. Was this the only gap, or just the one that got noticed? Medicines errors in care homes rarely have a single cause, and the manager wants to look at storage, stock, recording and competence together. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A senior spots a late dose on the MAR chart.
The person is checked and the error is reported as the procedure says.
The manager talks it through with the carer, kindly and clearly.
Nobody has looked at storage, stock or recording across the whole home.
Is anyone else rushing the night round, or signing before they give?
“We will tighten things up.” No owner, no date, no photo of the fix.
Nobody checks whether the changes were made or held.
“What did you do after the error, and how do you know it has not happened again?”

trail_close: Handling the error was the right first step. The gap is between that and a proper look at the whole system, with the follow through written down. Here is how CareStream helps you do that.

why.heading: One error is a prompt to check everything around it
why.sub: Looking only at the person misses the trolley, the stock, the handover and the paperwork.

cards.title: A slip often has company
cards.body: A late dose can sit next to a stock count that is out, a fridge that was not logged or a handover that skips medicines. One audit looks at all of it in one go.

cards.title: Promises need owners
cards.body: “We will tighten things up” is not a plan. Audit actions with a named owner, a due date and photo proof turn good intentions into something you can show.

cards.title: Fixes slip back without a re-check
cards.body: Without a second look, a change made in week one can quietly fade by week six. The next audit shows the last actions so you can mark each one fixed or not fixed.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We handled the error. Why run an audit as well?
items.a: Handling the error deals with the person and the moment. An audit looks at the system around it: storage, stock, recording and practice. It shows whether the slip was alone or one of several, and it leaves a record of what you checked.

Most homes start with Medicines Management for the monthly view and the Weekly Medication Stock and Storage check, with the daily audit for a short daily look. The Medication Competency Assessment looks at one staff member at a time.

items.q: Who can run the audit, and where?
items.a: Admins can run any audit. Staff can run the audits you tick for them. They use the Staff Hub, a web app that works on a phone, tablet or desktop. Admins also have the Audits page. You can schedule an audit to a named person with a due date and a repeat, and they are emailed reminders.

items.q: What happens to the things we find?
items.a: You add audit actions with an owner, a priority and a due date. Owners see them in the hub, mark them done and add photos as proof. If you are on a paid plan, recommendations can be drafted from your answers for you to edit and approve.

items.q: How do we know the fixes held?
items.a: At the next audit of the same kind, the earlier actions are listed. The auditor marks each one fixed or not fixed. If it is not fixed it reopens, and the owner is emailed. The Insights view also shows repeat failures across audits.

items.q: Does the audit train staff as well?
items.a: No, and that is deliberate. If the audit shows a practice gap, you can allocate an ad hoc training module on medication yourself, built from your own policy where it covers the topic. That is a manual step. Nothing is triggered automatically by an audit result.

items.q: Does this replace our incident report or medicines error procedure?
items.a: No. Reporting the error and following your own procedure still come first. The audit sits alongside them. It looks at the wider system and records what you did next.

items.q: What does it cost to try?
items.a: The audits are free on every plan, including the Free plan. You can create a free account and run one today, or look at pricing for the paid plans, which have a 14 day free trial.

limits.heading: A way to look at the system, not a replacement for your procedure

cards.title: It does not replace incident reporting
cards.body: An audit does not replace reporting the error or following your own medicines error procedure. Those come first. The audit looks at what sits around the error.

cards.title: The score is not a CQC rating
cards.body: Audit scores are CareStream's own and are not a regulator rating. An audit is also not a record submitted to any regulator. It is your own evidence of looking and acting.

cards.title: It does not teach or check hands on practice
cards.body: Observing a medicines round still needs a competent person watching. Recommendations and drafted action plans are on the paid plans only, and training after an audit is something you allocate yourself.

faqs.heading: Medication audits after an error, answered

items.q: What is a medication audit in a care home?
items.a: It is a structured check of how medicines are handled: supply, storage, administration, recording, controlled drugs and disposal. In CareStream, the Medicines Management audit covers these areas and gives a score by section.

items.q: How often should a medication audit care home routine run?
items.a: That is for the home to decide. Many use a daily or weekly short check and a fuller monthly audit. After an error you might run an extra audit sooner. You can schedule each one with a repeat and a named person.

items.q: Do I get an audit report I can keep?
items.a: Yes. A completed audit produces a PDF audit report with scores by section, answers, photos, the action plan and signatures. It is saved against the audit run and emailed to admins.

items.q: What should we do with audit actions?
items.a: Give each one an owner, a due date and a priority. Ask the owner to add a photo as proof when it is done. At the next audit, check each earlier action and mark it fixed or not fixed.
Yes. The audits, scoring, photos, PDF report, actions, scheduling and approval are free on every plan. Drafted recommendations are on the paid plans. Create a free account to try it.

items.q: Should we also review training after medication errors in care homes?
items.a: Often it helps. If the audit points to a practice gap, you can allocate a short ad hoc module from your Training screen, or point staff to the medication course. Both are steps you choose to take.

items.q: What do the regulations say about medicines?
items.a: Regulation 12 says care and treatment must be provided in a safe way, and its list includes "the proper and safe management of medicines". It does not set out an audit routine, so each provider decides how it checks.

items.q: What does CQC say about learning from medicines incidents?
items.a: The CQC guidance on Regulation 12 says incidents must be reviewed and thoroughly investigated by competent staff, and should lead to improvements. A recorded audit and its actions can show what you did after an error.

guide.heading: A practical way to audit after a medicines error
guide.lede: An audit after an error works best when it is calm, specific and short enough to finish. The aim is to learn from the error, not to look for someone to blame.

sections.h3: Look at the system around the error
paragraphs: Start with what happened, then widen out. A late dose may point to the timing of the round, the staffing on that shift, how stock is held or how the MAR chart is laid out. The CQC guidance on Regulation 12 says incidents should be reviewed and lead to improvements, and that staff involved should be told what was learned.
Keep the tone fair. Staff who fear blame stop reporting, and then you learn about the next slip later. Read our guide to MAR charts for new care staff if you want a plain refresher on recording.

sections.h3: Four steps that fit a busy service
checklist: Within a few days: run the Medicines Management audit, and add the Weekly Medication Stock and Storage check if storage is in question.
For every finding: add an action with an owner, a priority and a due date.
When an action is done: the owner adds a photo and a short note as proof.
At the next audit: mark each earlier action fixed or not fixed, and keep the audit report.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the error record, the audit report, the actions and the re-check together, so you can show what you found, what you changed and how you know it held.
